dataset_family: Rumailah Hospital geriatric and memory clinic, Hamad Medical Corporation / Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar, Doha, Qatar (recruited 2016-2020): 107 MCI analysed (33 progressed to dementia, 74 did not) plus 12 NCI controls
method_family: Corneal confocal microscopy (HRT-3 Rostock Cornea Module): manual sub-basal corneal nerve morphometry (CNFD, CNBD, CNFL). This is a peripheral (ophthalmic) nerve-fibre measure, not a brain measure. Comparator: NeuroQuant MRI volumetry (hippocampus, whole brain and 11 other structures, ICV-adjusted). Analysis: ROC/Youden cut-offs and covariate-adjusted binary logistic regression
what_it_shows: Within one MCI cohort, baseline corneal nerve measures and MRI volumetry were each tested for progression to dementia over a median 2.4 years. Volume was NOT preserved: progressors had lower hippocampal and whole-brain volume (p<0.0001). Volume also had the numerically higher AUC: 78% for hippocampus and 78% for whole brain, against 74% for CNFD, 73% for CNBD and 71% for CNFL (95% CIs overlap; the AUCs were not formally compared). Only accuracy at the Youden cut-offs favoured CCM (72-75% vs 68-69%), again with no test. In logistic models adjusted for hypertension, triglycerides, HDL and diabetes duration, abnormal CCM and abnormal volume were all significant (hippocampus OR 6.4, whole brain OR 7.5). After further adjustment for age and MoCA, abnormal CNFD (OR 6.1) and CNBD (OR 4.1) stayed significant. Abnormal hippocampal volume (OR 3.7, p=0.16) and whole-brain volume (OR 5.4, p=0.12) did not, though their point estimates were of similar size with wide CIs. MRI data were missing for 28 (26.2%) participants. No model entered CCM and volume together. The authors report that combining CCM with volumetry 'did not have any major impact'.
why:
Ponirakis et al. 2023, Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology 10(4):599-609, doi 10.1002/acn3.51747. The PDF title, author list and DOI match the summaries.md block and the map entry. The extract was read in full to the References: methods, results, Tables 1-3, discussion and limitations. PDF page N = journal page 598+N.

STATED FORM (Table A1): no. (1) Volume was not preserved or non-discriminative. Progressors had lower hippocampal and whole-brain volume at p<0.0001 (p.1, p.4), and both volumes predicted progression with AUC 78%, above every CCM measure (p.4, Table 2 p.7). (2) The comparison does not show volume to be 'late' or 'insufficient'. Unadjusted, and adjusted for vascular covariates, abnormal hippocampal and whole-brain volume carried significant odds of progression (p.6-7). They lost significance only once age and MoCA were added, with wide CIs, in a smaller MRI sample (26.2% missing MRI, p.7). The authors themselves read this as volume loss being 'associated with age' (p.8). (3) Scope: CCM images peripheral corneal nerves, described by the authors as 'a surrogate imaging marker for neurodegeneration' (p.2). It is not one of the statement's brain measure families (functional, microstructural, mechanical, metabolic) unless 'microstructural' is read to include peripheral nerve.

NARROWED FORM (round 20): partly. The study runs its own head-to-head of a non-volumetric measure against hippocampal and whole-brain volumetry for MCI-to-dementia progression. The narrowed wording's parity and 'information volume did not carry' strands are each met only weakly. (a) Parity: CCM AUC was 74% (64-85) against 78% (67-89) and 78% (66-91) for volume. The CIs overlap, but the point estimates favour volume, and the AUCs were never tested against each other. The ROC for volume appears to rest on the participants with MRI (28 missing), so the two ROCs are not strictly on the same sample. 'At least as well as' holds only for accuracy at cut-offs (72-75% vs 68-69%), which is untested. (b) Information beyond volume: the evidence is covariate-adjusted independence. After age and MoCA adjustment, CNFD and CNBD stayed significant and volume did not (Table 3, p.7). No model included both CCM and volume, and the combined-marker AUCs (CNFD + hippocampus 75.6%) did not exceed hippocampal volume alone (78%). The authors state that combining 'did not have any major impact' (p.8). So incremental value over volume is not demonstrated. It is also not the same comparison as P-478, where stiffness added to volume in a joint model. (c) Consistent with the narrowed wording's last sentence, hippocampal volume remained discriminative here. (d) The peripheral-measure scope question in (3) above applies equally to the narrowed wording, which enumerates functional, mechanical and microstructural measures. Whether a corneal nerve-fibre measure belongs to that set is for the operator to decide. If it is excluded, the verdict becomes 'no'.

INDEPENDENCE: Qatar clinic cohort. It shares no dataset, site or authors with the current supporters (P-518 Sunshine Coast, P-478 Delaware, P-432 Bristol, P-460 meta-analysis, P-584 PREVENT-AD, P-581 NACC) or with the other candidates (P-44 Busan, P-1107 Tainan, P-183 ADNI). No current supporter uses this method family. No other Ponirakis/Malik paper was found in summaries.md by author search. Not a preprint. Not in registry_duplicates.json.

The block's 'CCM measures outperformed hippocampal and whole-brain volumetry' overstates the source: the AUCs favour volume. Quotes are rejoined across line breaks, with ligatures, en dashes and inequality signs normalised to ASCII; superscript citation numbers (e.g. in the p.2 quote) are omitted. The extract dropped the plus-minus signs in the descriptive statistics, so no quote here relies on them.

quotes.quote: Progressors had lower corneal nerve measures, hippocampal, and whole brain volume (all p < 0.0001). However, CCM had a higher prognostic accuracy (72%-75% vs 68%-69%) for identifying individuals who progressed to dementia compared to hippocampus and whole brain volume.

We have pioneered the technique of corneal confocal microscopy (CCM), a rapid non-invasive ophthalmic imaging technique that enables quantification of corneal nerve morphology as a surrogate imaging marker for neurodegeneration in a range of peripheral neuropathies and central neurodegenerative diseases.

The area under the curve (AUC) to predict progression to dementia was 74% (95% CI 64-85%, p < 0.0001) for CNFD, 73% (95% CI 63%-84%, p < 0.0001) for CNBD, 71% (95% CI 61%-82%, p < 0.0001) for CNFL, 63% (95% CI 51%-74%, p < 0.05) for the CNBD/CNFD ratio, 78% (95% CI 67%-89%, p < 0.0001) for hippocampal volume, 78% (95% CI 66%-91%, p < 0.0001) for whole brain volume
CCM measures had a higher prognostic accuracy for identifying participants who progressed to dementia compared to hippocampus and whole brain volume (72%-75% vs 68%-69%).

The odds ratio (OR) for progression from MCI to dementia adjusted for hypertension, triglycerides, HDL and diabetes duration was 6.3 times (95% CI: 2.0-20.2) higher with abnormal CNFD (<=25 no./mm2), 5.8 times (95% CI: 1.9-18.1) higher with abnormal CNBD (<=44 no./mm2), 4.4 times (95% CI: 1.5-13.2) higher with abnormal CNFL (<=15 mm/mm2), 6.4 times (95% CI: 1.4-30.0) higher with abnormal hippocampus volume (<=0.44 ICV%), and 7.5 times (95% CI: 1.4-40.9) higher with abnormal whole brain volume (<=72 ICV%).

The OR for progression to dementia after adjusting for age, MoCA, hypertension, triglycerides, HDL and diabetes duration remained 6.1 (95% CI: 1.6-23.8) times higher with abnormal CNFD and 4.1 (95% CI: 1.2-14.2) times higher with abnormal CNBD but was no longer significant with abnormal CNFL (2.3, 95% CI: 0.7-8.3, p = 0.19), hippocampus (3.7, 95% CI: 0.6-22.5, p = 0.16), and whole brain volume (5.4, 95% CI: 0.7-44.6, p = 0.12) (Table 3 and Fig. 2). The sensitivity analysis where missing MRI data were coded as unknown (n = 28, 26.2%) gave similar results

The AUC of a combined abnormal CNFD (<=25 no./mm2) and abnormal hippocampus volume (<=0.44 ICV%) or abnormal whole brain volume (<=72 ICV%) were 75.6% (95% CI 63%-88%) and 72.4% (95% CI 60%-85%), respectively.
Certainly, CCM has an independent prognostic ability compared to hippocampus and whole brain volume. Combining CCM measures with brain volumetry did not have any major impact.
This suggests that corneal nerve loss is a more direct measure of early neurodegeneration in MCI, whilst the loss of brain volume was associated with age but not with progression to dementia.

We acknowledge the relatively small cohort size, short duration of follow up and the lack of more rigorous measures and biomarkers of AD, including cortical Ab-42 or tau PET, CSF Ab-42 or phosphorylated tau, CSF T-tau or FDG PET hypometabolism.
